subject: Hosted tunnel cert bridge and DNS shadowing plan
messages:
From: Liam O'Connor <ops@acme-retail.com>
To: Rachel Kim <rachel_kim@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-05-17T08:14:00-07:00
Subject: Hosted tunnel TLS: current certs + split-DNS question

Hi Rachel,

Quick one from our side: we've been running a hosted tunnel from our VPC into Redwood's private deployment for a group of internal services. Attached is a CSV of the certs we currently present on that tunnel (acme_tls_inventory.csv).

Two questions:
- We want Redwood to terminate TLS at your edge for this tunnel, but still present our internal service FQDNs to client apps (split-horizon DNS on our side). Is there a recommended pattern to preserve client trust without exposing our internal DNS externally?
- If Redwood acts as a TLS bridge/proxy, what are the constraints on cert chains (intermediates, OCSP, stapling) and preferred rotation cadence?

We're trying to avoid a hard cutover for ~30 internal teams; ideally a gradual handover with no client config changes.

Thanks,
Liam O'Connor
Infrastructure Lead, Acme Retail

High level ask from my side: we need a plan that keeps client TLS semantics unchanged (SNI + cert presented as their internal FQDN) while allowing Redwood to front the connection for observability and autoscaling reasons. Can you share which services rely on internal-only SRV records vs plain FQDNs? That will help decide whether we can do SNI passthrough vs TLS termination+/bridge.

Date: 2028-05-17T11:30:00-07:00
Subject: RE: Hosted tunnel TLS: current certs + split-DNS question

Hey all — drafted three practical approaches and tradeoffs. Attached: draft-rotation-runbook.md + a quick architecture sketch (architecture-diagram.png).

Option A — SNI passthrough at tunnel edge
- Redwood performs TCP passthrough; client TLS terminates at customer backend.
- Pros: zero cert changes on clients, minimal trust changes.
- Cons: limited observability for token-level tracing, harder to autoscale individual services.

Option B — TLS bridge (recommended middle ground)
- Redwood terminates TLS at the tunnel ingress, then establishes an internal TLS connection to the customer backend. Redwood re-presents the customer's FQDN to downstream by using SNI rewrite and presenting either the customer's cert (provided) or a short-lived cert we mint that chains to a customer-trusted intermediate.
- Pros: preserves client-facing FQDNs, enables per-route observability and caching, allows progressive rollout.
- Cons: requires agreement on intermediate trust, OCSP/CRL handling, and a rotation runbook.

Option C — Full customer termination + proxy metadata header
- Customer keeps full TLS termination; Redwood only proxies metadata over a separate secure channel.
- Pros: simplest for trust.
- Cons: requires client config updates and reduces feature parity.

Operational requirements for TLS bridge (Option B)
- Customer provides: private CA chain or accepts a Redwood-intermediate signed by their root (offline CSR exchange).
- OCSP/ stapling: Redwood will staple OCSP for the certs it presents; we need an OCSP responder reachable or an agreed cache TTL.
- Key custody: HSM or KMS-backed keys for any long-lived signing material. Short-lived certs (<24h) are preferred for automatic revocation resilience.
- Split-horizon DNS: customer can either expose a private DNS view accessible from Redwood via the tunnel, or provide a hostmap (internal FQDN -> IP) file we can use in the bridge.

Next steps I propose:
1) Decide Option B vs A by EOW (May 19).
2) If Option B: exchange an offline CSR and draft the rotation runbook (attached) and schedule a dry-run.
3) Confirm whether Acme will allow OCSP responder access or accept stapling by Redwood.

Questions for Acme: do you have an internal DNS resolver we can query over the tunnel, or will you provide an authoritative zone dump?

—Marissa
Marissa Cole
Product Manager, Private Deployments

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>

Date: 2028-05-18T10:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Hosted tunnel TLS: current certs + split-DNS question

Thanks Marissa — good breakdown. A few technical clarifications from cert-ops: 

- OCSP stapling: if Redwood staples OCSP responses we need reliable fresher caches. For short-lived certs we can avoid long OCSP dependencies, but if Acme's issuing CA requires OCSP, we must ensure Redwood can reach the responder or the CA can provide signed stapled responses via an API.
- CRL vs OCSP: CRLs are brittle for high-volume services; prefer OCSP with stapling and a fallback to a short TTL cached status.
- Client cert validation: some Acme services use mTLS for backend calls. If we terminate at our edge, we must either forward client cert information (x-ssl-client-* headers) and preserve identity or perform mutual TLS with client certs passed through. Need to know which backends require mutual auth.
- Rotation: recommend two-step rotation window: publish new intermediate to customer 72h prior, cut traffic over during low hours with rolling restart. We'll provide a dry-run playbook.

From Marissa's diagram: if we use hostmaps, ensure they are signed and versioned (hash in runbook) so we can safely revert.

I can take point on the rotation playbook and will coordinate with Neha to run the dry-run.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
To: Rachel Kim <rachel_kim@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Liam O'Connor <ops@acme-retail.com>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-05-18T16:40:00-07:00
Subject: Decisions: TLS bridge approved with constraints

Following the discussion and after reviewing the inventory, Redwood will proceed with Option B (TLS bridge) for Acme's hosted tunnel with the following constraints and actions: 

1) Trust model: Acme will either provide an intermediate CA signed by their root or accept a Redwood-managed intermediate that chains to an agreed customer-trusted root. We will not present certificates signed by a Redwood public CA.
2) OCSP/Stapling: Acme must provide an OCSP responder endpoint reachable over the tunnel, or allow Redwood to cache signed OCSP responses from their CA. Redwood will staple responses and monitor freshness.
3) DNS: Acme will expose a private DNS resolver over the tunnel (preferred). If not possible, they will provide a versioned hostmap (signed) for the service FQDNs.
4) Key custody: long-lived signing keys must be KMS/HSM-backed. For any short-lived certs we mint, Redwood will use ephemeral KMS keys and automatic rotation (<24h).
5) Runbook & dry-run: Karthik + Neha will execute a dry-run the week of 2028-05-24. We will schedule a 2-hour maintenance window with Acme and run traffic mirroring to validate no client breakage.

@Liam — please confirm whether Acme can expose an internal resolver over the tunnel and whether you can provide an OCSP responder URL. Once confirmed we'll exchange CSRs and finalize the runbook (JIRA INF-8721).

Thanks — Jonas
Jonas Weber
Head of Private Deployments, Redwood Inference
